extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, attorneys, and respondents in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for filing and prevailing on a Request for Reconsideration of a USPTO Director's Final Order in Office of Enrollment and Discipline matters under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c). Covers grounds (new evidence or error of law/fact), timeliness/filing method, evidentiary expectations, and limitations on relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for Reconsideration (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may grant a request for reconsideration or modification of the Director's Final Order if the request is based on newly discovered evidence, or an error of law or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory gate: a request must specifically be grounded in newly discovered evidence or an identifiable error of law or fact to be considered. Mere disagreement with the Final Order is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow Standard of Review — Extraordinary Remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for reconsideration are subject to a very high standard of review and are extraordinary remedies that should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office applies a narrow standard similar to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rules 59(e)/60(b). Courts have limited reconsideration to extraordinary circumstances (e.g., the court has patently misunderstood a party, made a decision outside the adversarial issues, or made an error of apprehension). Authorities cited include Hutchinson v. Staton, Above the Belt, Inc. v. Mel Bohannan Roofing, Inc., and other federal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly Discovered Evidence Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new evidence submitted must not have been available or discoverable before issuance of the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requestor must demonstrate that the evidence could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)). Evidence that was available prior to entry of judgment is not a basis for reconsideration. Unsupported assertions are inadequate — documentary proof (e.g., bank records, correspondence) and explanation of prior unavailability/due diligence are required. Cases cited: Boryan v. United States; Frederick S. Wyle P.C. v. Texaco.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors of Law or Fact Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain reconsideration the requester must identify specific errors of law or fact in the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General disagreement, relitigating previously presented arguments, or rehashing the record is insufficient. The error must be more than a difference in interpretation; examples where reconsideration might be appropriate include clear mistakes in apprehension or decisions outside the issues presented. Citations: Hutchinson, Arthur v. King, Wadley v. Park at Landmark, Above the Belt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and Method of Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for Reconsideration must be filed within 20 days of the decision and comply with filing instructions stated in the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order may specify method and address for filing (e.g., mailed to the General Counsel). Failure to comply with stated filing requirements (timeliness or method) can be an independent basis for rejecting the Request. Example: filing by email when the Final Order required mailing may be rejected if the mailed copy was not received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary Support and Burden of Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a request for reconsideration must be supported by evidence and authority; unsupported allegations will not overcome unrebutted record evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When challenging factual findings (e.g., sufficiency of bank funds, issuance of debit/credit cards, calculation of fees), the appellant must submit corroborating documents (bank statements, correspondence) and show why such evidence was not available earlier. Unrebutted hearing evidence will control unless credible new proof is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on Use — Not a Vehicle for Reargument
rubrics_metrics.description: A Request for Reconsideration is not a vehicle to restate disagreement with a final judgment or to relitigate matters that were or could have been raised earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts uniformly hold that motions under Rules 59(e) and 60 are not to be used to relitigate old matters, present arguments that could have been made earlier, or furnish an unhappy litigant a second chance. Examples and citations: Hutchinson; Arthur v. King; Wadley v. Park at Landmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of Restitution — Reliance on Record Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Restitution amounts are based on the unrebutted evidence in the record about fees/surcharges paid by the affected client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To change restitution, the requester must present evidence or authority showing an error in the calculation (e.g., authoritative proof that a different fee applied). Absent such evidence, the Director's calculation based on the record stands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible Sanction Elements and Practical Limits (Customer Number and Access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Director may order dissociation of a practitioner's name from USPTO customer numbers and preclude obtaining a customer number until reinstatement, but such an order should not prevent filing or prosecuting pro se applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without a Customer Number, an individual may file pro se via EFS-Web (without non-electronic filing surcharge) or by fax/paper submissions per 37 C.F.R. §§ 1.6(c),(d), 1.16(t), and may be disadvantaged in convenience (e.g., lack of Private PAIR access) but not prevented from filing. Challenges that such restrictions violate regulations (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 1.31) must consider these alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional Conduct Standards Cited (Ethics Violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific disciplinary rules relied on to assess misconduct include: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3); 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4); 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5); and 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions proscribe: failing to properly or timely remit funds from a client to the Office (10.23(c)(3)); engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (10.23(b)(4)); engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (10.23(b)(5)); and neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner (10.77(c)). The ALJ found violations of these rules based on repeatedly submitting a declined debit card, allowing a client's application to go abandoned, and failing to advise the client.
